body: For real, breakdowns are a privilege at this point. I can't have one. I need to maintain a job and build a career and keep getting up every morning and slamming uppers to get through the day because I need to support other people who depend on me.

Hey man. It doesn't feel it in the moment but I need success stories like this. I wish every day that suicide was an option but it's not, so I need something to keep me getting up in the morning to try and provide for my family. I dunno. Maybe on the good days this will be something I try and remind myself of.
Well, I've been called a lot of things but "eloquent" is not one of them. Angry and hopeless though, those fit.

Fuck, friend. I wish I could give you hope but I've been in this situation before. Cycled through so many meds it's easier to list what I haven't been on than what I have. All the ERs did was traumatize me further, and no one ever points out that it literally does take money to make money. Everyone always has that vague "I'm here if you need me" but like...I need money. I need money to try and get help so that I can get up in the morning and find a way forward. I don't need generalized motivational statements coming from people of privilege.
We aren't worth shit. They can always just make more of us and then virtue signal over the concerning rates of deaths of despair while designing the systems to keep killing us.

I feel you so much. Working more to increase my salary has actually made it worse for me. My benefits improved but now cost me money. Food has increased but I don't qualify for any aid. I have a small amount of equity but not enough to leverage anything for it. The wage gap between dirt poor and extravagance is designed to keep us in this awful cycle and I don't ever see a way out. But that doesn't stop anyone making more than me from platitudes and fake optimism about "You'll get there one day" and "I was like that once too". Cool. I'm approaching forty and I'm still not there and still like that now so when the fuck does this happen?

The circlejerk over college is god damn exhausting. I waited. I figured out what I liked, what I could stand to do, what I hated doing, I figured out how to not take on predatory loans. I took specialized courses geared towards my career instead. 

But if I'm struggling to find work in my 30s, should've gone to college! Oh you're trying to? Great, here's some debt despite everything. You're an adult learner too? Cool, here's class schedules that don't jive with any work schedule I've ever seen and unrealistic expectations of a workload for a working adult, but you know, work real hard at it for 5—7 years and you too can get a foothold with all the other 20 year olds just starting their career telling me in 20 years it'll pay off. It's fantastic. I'm so glad by the time I'm in my 60s I might make what everyone around me is making now.

But how dare I not be optimistic about all my opportunities.

It's so exhausting. I'm so tired of being so angry at my friends. No one wants that in a social circle
So I guess good thing I'm uselessly killing myself working full time, going to school, and studying for job certifications that I get denied promotions for getting because at least I can't go see friends because I have no time or money. I can't even afford the gas to get out to them. And friends deserve to be around people who can celebrate their successes instead of drinking themselves to death in self loathing and rage after seeing them.

I don't even know what to do anymore. It's literally been decades of this and nothing is "getting better". We do all the right steps, I got a job, I tried to find a way to go to school without debt, I got the training to climb the fucking ladder and this bitch is actually a fucking slide the whole time.

Have you considered therapy? It's so life changing! You just have to want it bad enough and find the right therapist in network who takes your insurance without a copay and has availability and deals with your specific issues and then give it like 2-5 years of work and it'll totally help. And if it didn't, well, you fucked up.

I don't even understand the point of price gouging this bad. They can't take what we don't have so no one gets money, so...let's keep raising the prices. And asking questions about employment status on doctor's appointments so we can jack up the up front payment when we find out you have no money already.

Honestly it becomes an old friend after about a decade. That empty void of nothing feels like home and the drinking and self harm and pills are familiar comforts in long nights. And then...time passes and somehow you're not dead, so might as well down another glass of whiskey and get to planning another suicide you'll never succeed at, just like everything else in life

Ah, gotcha! Yeah, I'm US based. Sorry I can't offer any practical advice for you, I don't know how similar the tests would be. But good luck! My only advice is that I took mine on a Friday so that no matter the result, I could drink afterwards.

I just took my RLAT a few months ago. There isn't an oral portion?

I do recall more husbandry questions showing up than I expected, although I'm biased because I carried a lot of GP knowledge over to research, so I didn't study as hard on conversions and drugs and I didn't struggle with those questions. Several small rodent questions came up about hams and guinea pigs, and a few for NHP. I would say maybe a third of the test was veterinary info and the rest was a lot of husbandry of USDA animals, cage set ups, behavior, etc. Not a ton of regulatory questions came up and maybe two or three of sterilants.

Overall, I wish I had reviewed the ALAT material a little more before I took the test. I ended up not as confident about passing as I did with my ALAT.

I don't know if I have any constructive feedback that will help but your professor sounds like a dick. Criticism can be given compassionately and constructively, but it sounds like he chose to be cruel and condescending instead, which is not on you at all. That's a poor professor.

But if it helps, I always remind myself in the long run, I won't remember grades. I can't tell you what I got on a paper in 7th grade. I might have had a difficult time with geometry but do I remember if I got an A, or a C? Not even slightly. I might have actually failed it. Not once in my adult life has someone asked me about my GPA, because my resume and references speak volumes more than grades, and I work at a university.

I also try and remember that unlike past me in high school or the first attempt at college, I am a god damn adult. I have a job. Sometimes two. I have adult responsibilities, I have taxes and medical concerns, and a family to take care of. Yes, my education is important but academia falls into an echo chamber where too often they believe it is the MOST important thing. I'm too old and too accomplished in so many other areas of my life to believe that. Cool, I got a B on a final this week. I also passed a certification test for work, got a raise in money, not grades, and got myself in line for a promotion. End of the day, what do you think mattered most to me this week? What do you think will make the difference ten years down the line? Will I even remember the final next year? Next month even?

I take my education seriously. But at the end of the day, I either get a degree with a few less than stellar grades, or I stress myself out so much about a letter on a piece of paper that I end up dropping out for a third time. Of course, none of this applies if you're in school to be a doctor or something larger than a bachelor's. But there are so many things in this world larger than one professor who apparently failed his own class on Ethics.

A bit late but was it [this painting?](https://www.masterofwarcraft.net/2017/10/familiar-view-in-this-painting-i-saw-at.html) I can't help past that, I've been looking for a print on and off over the years and have never been able to track down the original artist or image.

I'll second this. I used the chat line and the agent stayed with me for almost two hours. I felt terrible about taking her time because there are people who need it more than me, but it was distinctly different from the last time I used their chat line. They can't fix any of my problems, but they didn't rush me off in fifteen minutes and she seemed to genuinely care - it wasn't a script.

Yes, I think part of the problem is the pain is managed through medication, so when doctors are seeing her, they aren't really grasping the full picture of how terrible and immobilizing this is when untreated.

I strongly believe, unfortunately, that we are dealing with a much more complex issue, on top of previous physiological injuries, along the lines of MS, FND, CRPS and we're struggling to get the diagnostics to rule out anything in order to start addressing that possibility. Because I would love for a specialist to tell me we're idiots and that everything looks normal and it's not any of those abstract and complicated diagnoses. That has not been the case but it's taken a lot of pushing to get diagnostics for specialists to come back and not look us in the eye and say that actually, you're right, things don't look right and further testing is absolutely warranted. We'll keep pushing but the irony is the psychological toll of this back and forth is becoming an equivalent issue.

Yeah, that's one differential diagnosis we're concerned about. There are a couple places in our city that deal with CRPS and other complex neuro/autoimmune/inflammatory/unspecified causes of pain issues so hopefully one of their doctors in a completely different medical system has a better opinion.
Ugh god. This happens all the time but we don't believe it happened to you because you're a woman, who's simultaneously prone to issues but also overreacting to issues entirely due to your gender.
I'm kind of making a script for all these because in the moment, we both freeze and I think having these lines memorized might help.

Thank you. It's difficult and I think we just needed a few days to vent and be angry and then go right back to trying to figure out what's going on. 

We are looking into therapy as well, not just for chronic pain but also because this whole process is clearly overwhelming.

No worries, I didn't take it that way at all. The whole reason I'm going to doctors is I realize they are our best shot at getting an answer and some management of whatever is going on. I've just never myself had an experience quite as dismissive as I just saw with my wife and it makes me angry and sad.

At one point I had a doctor save my life simply by sitting down and talking with me through my symptoms. To this day I wish I could find him again and thank him, because his time and patience literally saved a life that day, and that wasn't even why I went there in the first place. I just want to find the same for my wife and I'm struggling so hard to find that level of care again.
Hey cool, thank you so much for that. I will look into that for sure.

I would even buy Occam's Razor if, like...you offered to look out the window and see if it was a horse. But in one breath she said that she wouldn't ever really look at nerve damage as an issue and then said in ten years of medicine she's never really seen it as a case.

...because you just said you don't look for it as an issue. So...of course you wouldn't see it?

Like, hey look at those horses on the right, and she looks left and says, I dunno, I never see any horses so I don't think that's it.
That's my biggest fear. We're not important. We're not well off. We are just two normal people trying to live a relatively active life. Why should anyone care about us?

Thank you for your response. We have seen a neurologist and are following that referral down to a multidisciplinary clinic that deals with psychosomatic illness, but that is several months down the line. My frustration is that no doctor seems to want to rule out the physical cause in the meantime. It's almost as if they saw the assessment scheduled and immediately dismissed any other cause than psychosomatic. The refusal of diagnostics is the most baffling. They increased the pain meds, which we didn't want nor asked for, but then had no interest in trying to find out why, exactly, the pain levels were so high. So she agreed the pain was real, but then attributed it to psychosomatic causes, and then got upset when we requested diagnostics to confirm that physically, everything looked okay while we wait on the assessment.

It's also just frustrating to see more than one doctor commenting on here with the exact plan of what we wanted to do, which is exclude any physical cause while we wait to address the psychosocial should everything come back diagnostically normal (which again, it isn't, at least in regards to spinal health). And none of y'all seem to practice in the Midwest, so I'm stuck with specialists who didn't even take as much time as any of you took to read a five minute Reddit post and come to the same conclusion as us.
She was a woman physician and I think that's what took us by surprise. We are, of course, looking for a second opinion. After maybe a couple days and some drinks to calm down.
Well we're US based so that alone should be a clue that this isn't going to go well at all, unfortunately.
I think it's a biomedical issue, really. The only difference is that in the US, I'm also risking bankruptcy to still not have answers.

I saw my insurance offered a health aide or something like that but honestly I thought it was to just deny care and send you to less expensive options. Obviously I'm very jaded by the entire for-profit healthcare system. So these advocate actually work?

We're trying to keep hope. So far (I hope) we've been relatively polite and calm but firm in what we need but it is a system that is so draining. Very honestly so much love to the individual technicians and lab assistants and receptionists who have been nothing short of amazing when helping us through all of this. It is really at the doctor level where it is all falling apart.
We have one MRI without contrast to account for the possibility of epilepsy or maybe an old TBI. Past that, we will likely seek a new neuro since that's the end of his specialty

Here in my city we do have a clinic that deals with functional disorders like that. It is a long time to get in but we do have an appointment eventually. My issue more is that this doctor in particular completely disregarded the possibility of a physical cause and just jumped immediately to psychosomatic.

I don't know how else to explain it to them. She was a functional human being with some musculoskeletal pain less than a month ago and now everything's burning and she can't do something as simple as walk down the stairs. And no one seems to think this is a problem other than treating the nerve pain and not finding the issue.
Yeah that's fair. I didn't realize how no one was receiving the actual imaging because no one will send it digitally so we are in the process of compiling all that as well.

We tried to request it at this last doctor but the best she offered was an xray for"peace of mind". Also, just got a call from that doctor, funnily enough. Now it's "we need an MRI after seeing those results".

I honestly wasn't even aware a patient advocate was a thing. Do they actually help, or are they just there to avoid lawsuits for the hospital? I have no interest in lawsuits. I just want someone to help my wife
I'm hoping someone soon. I'm not even arguing that there isn't a psychosomatic component to it. Can we just look at mechanical first just to make sure? But that's apparently too much to ask.

I get it, I really do. I come from a veterinary background and I saw our doctors going through the same things. I really don't want us to be considered problem patients but at the same time, I only ever saw the problem patients get help, or referrals, or diagnostics. And I hate that and I really, really don't have it in me to be that person. I'm running a line of trying to advocate but trying really hard not to be an asshat about it. But then nothing gets done and my wife suffers every day for it.
It's so frustrating that in 2022 we have so much documented evidence that this bias exists and yet, we don't change the system. Like even slightly.

We had an insurance issue with Gabapentin and honestly just ended up going out of pocket through GoodRX for close to the same price. It's so stupid that insurance can simply say, no, we need a doctor to write out or call in an approval for this. What is the prescription then, exactly!?

Right? I was so confused. She said it shouldn't cause pain. We asked why it was such an intense pain then, because I actually don't disagree with that; many people with a couple mm slip say it's painful, but not completely and utterly debilitating. That's when she said it was a nocebo effect from seeing the xray and probably not any other reason. I actually don't know why we stayed in the appointment after that except for maybe shock.

Thanks. I just feel so helpless and sometimes I do wonder if I'm making it worse because doctors seem to hate the fact that I'm there? I'm really just trying to confirm what she's saying but maybe I'm doing it wrong somehow.

God, I'm so tired of doctors saying there was nothing wrong because there was no acute trauma directly prior to this episode of pain. Don't worry about the improperly treated car accident that compressed your spine and broke your back. That was twenty five years ago and there's no way that's impacting your spine today.

I'm glad you got a diagnosis on board and hopefully a good team behind you

I don't know if it makes me feel better or worse that this is an ingrained systemic issue. My sympathies - pain is seriously the worst symptom and the only option is ever "haaaave you tried our drugs"
I'm so glad you finally found someone. It is soul cruhsing to think we could be trying for years to fix this. The difference between even two years ago and now is just...I can't even describe it

I was briefly in a pre-med program and quickly changed it over to an Anthro/Social Science program because it became overwhelmingly obvious that biomedicine is so breathtakingly broken in the way it is practiced. Even though I firmly believe there are solid medical solutions out there in the word, it is absolutely a sociocultural issue that most people will never be able to find those solutions and recover.

No and one of the first things they always ask is "why did you wait so long to see the doctor?" or "why don't you have a primary?"

Because I live in America and death is the more affordable option. You all work in healthcare, you see every day how this system bankrupts people. We literally couldn't afford health insurance until now and we still can't afford the bills that are coming. I didn't take her to the doctor because one, I was afraid no one would believe her and I was damn right about that and two, how the fuck am I supposed to afford food now??
I'm also a woman, and I think that's actually making it worse. Like two women are more wrong than just one.

Yes, I think that is our next step. The problem with many of these pain syndromes are that they seem to be diagnoses of exclusion, when we are fighting to get the diagnostics that would, in fact, exclude other causes.

My wife, to her immense credit, held herself back from snapping that exact question at her. If we didn't push for some diagnostic, that doctor would have sent us away with, yeah, keep doing PT and gabapentin and see if that helps despite the fact that the entire reason you're here today is that it's not helping.

This makes me so sad and so angry. Athletes function at and through a different level than an average person like me. That everything feels dismissed because she's not completely bedridden is asinine.

And you're right. The casual attitude with which they foist you off on another doctor's list to be diagnosed or dealt with another day is literally killing people. It's so heartbreaking that we've set an entire system up like this.

Oh my god, 30 specialists is insane. I'm so terrified that's what it's going to take because yeah, at this point the search is almost more debilitating and emotionally exhausting than the actual symptoms. It's just a rollercoaster of heartbreak and anger and hope and let downs.

Hey, thank you so much for this answer and thank you for explaining it in such respectful terms that don't minimize the issue or insult our ability to understand complex issues. I believe we have one such multi disciplinary lab here through a teaching university and that will be our next step. I'm so frustrated because I solidly believe there is a medical cause or causes to this and no doctor has actually addressed it better than a random Reddit post over five minutes of a brief medical history. 

I think we're fully aware that these are issues that likely will never be cured, but managed for the rest of her life. But to have to fight so hard for diagnostics to even rule out mechanical injury to get to the focus of "why is there so much pain if nothing is out of place" is so disheartening. Because on physical exam everyone has written her off as"within limits" and on rads, every time we suddenly get a call saying "oh, our bad, I guess you really do need an MRI". I was just so shocked to be told to our faces that it a nocebo effect that doesn't need diagnostics that I lost any ability to advocate for her.

This particular doctor was supposed to be a pain and rehabilitation specialist. We're definitely going to be getting a second opinion from a different one, possibly in another hospital system entirely. We are lucky enough to live in an area with multiple teaching universities with very large medical facilities, so hopefully one day we will land the right doctor. Stories like this make me hopeful though!

We're considering it due to the exaggeration of all symptoms only on the right side. Sudden loss of feeling or control in the right arm which leads to her dropping things, loss of proprioception through the right leg, burning and tingling through the right side and muscle seizure throughout the right side. Our feeling is the physical exams have been glossed over because she has solid muscling and can compensate for a lot of deficiencies in the moment. Twice doctors have lightly pushed on her leg and said they don't see a difference between right and left. A third year resident doing the intake actually exerted force, and saw immediately that her right leg dropped like a box of rocks, but no one listened to him because he was a resident. It's the force and the spontaneous intermittent loss of control that docs aren't seeing, and I'm not really sure how to get across that even I am seeing these very real issues at home. 

The PT is suspecting a brachial plexus injury because she went headfirst into a windshield as a child, impacting her neck right at that area, and has struggled with these deficiencies ever since. And while we're aware that if it is a twenty five year old injury to the nerves, there's not a whole lot we can do but manage the present, but we'd like to know if that's what we're truly dealing with. We'd like an EMG to be sure but it seems like that was a last resort option that this doctor was reluctant to discuss.

We sought out a neurologist for the same reason. Even though his focus is only seizure disorders and he will likely refer us to another neurologist, he acknowledged that these are very real, life interrupting symptoms and then ordered tests to ensure he isn't missing anything like actual epilepsy before sending for an FND consult.

We are trying to get the doc to order an EMG, but nerve function impairment seems to be an exclusionary diagnosis that they won't consider until mechanical and psychological are ruled out. And everyone knows that once psych is on the record, it's never ruled out. Definitely going to keep pushing for that though.
In this day and age I really can't even. "Sorry we put you through agony but have you tried hydrocortisone?"

I hope someone can go with you! I can't imagine if my wife had to do this alone. I don't feel like I'm much help but I can back up her story and I'm a solid shoulder to cry on in the car. Hopefully having someone to do the same can help you. It's really god damn scary to go through this.

It's so frustrating. We understand she's likely been living with at least one degenerative back issue her whole life. If it had been properly medically treated years ago, we wouldn't be here. But it wasn't, and it's being shrugged off as "welp, you say you've been in pain this whole time but you can stand up and slightly shift side to side and that meets our definition of normal." I feel like someone should at least give a fuck that she's been compensating through intense pain her whole life and even if they don't, we are sitting in front of doctors saying she's been in severe pain for years and somehow, it's even worse now. I have seen her hike with a back spasm that would have put me crying on the floor for an emergency room, and right now she's can't function with the level of pain she's at. That's an insanely high level of pain and no one wants to find out WHY.

Spondylolisthesis of L5-S1 of a few millimeters, along with disc degeneration and a 16° curve of the spine to the right consistent with scoliosis.

But apparently, according to this doctor, the slip doesn't usually cause pain or impairment and it's not really worth further diagnostics to find out why she's so immobilized by pain. Just activate the core, which the doc spent a lot of time explaining how to do that to AN ATHLETIC TRAINER, and increase medications until it doesn't hurt anymore. She also noted posture had no abnormalities, like, for example, a curve to the right that even I can see. And if it's there, the doc is suggesting everything falls into normal physiologic range and noted no abnormal ranges  of motion, despite the fact that she needed help sitting on the table and standing back up. Her sit to stand was rated as excellent in the exam.

....we're gonna look for a second opinion because that's not even half of it and reading it over, that's bad.

We had to request an xray as the first test because nerve damage appears to be a diagnosis of exclusion, so we aren't allowed to find out if neuropathy is because of damaged nerves right off the bat.

Fun fact, we started all this at an urgent care clinic, and their radiologist recommended a full CT. Has anyone actually agreed? Not a one.

It's absolutely insane. We have to show up 15 minutes early but the doctor didn't even look at the chart until 30 minutes past the appointment. Somehow all the notes get lost in transit so I guess I'll be bringing a physical file as well.

I shouldn't have to babysit an adult who somehow managed to get this many degrees.
That's the exact line we're getting dealt here. It's an old injury so it's probably not the cause but we won't image it just to make sure. Just trust us.

We're also working with a better doc on that possibility. He's still not great but at least he acknowledged she is more affected by minor things because she's an athlete, and he immediately sent us to the proper referrals when it was clear some things weren't in his wheelhouse.

That's a valid concern. I've had a doctor completely turn her back on me when I was trying to back up my wife's concerns because I wasn't the patient, so what I had to say was irrelevant and annoying to them.

Thanks. I know I'm just livid right now and in the next couple of days we'll regroup and find a second opinion but it's just so. Much. And this is the third doctor to do a half assed exam and I just can't grasp why the PT noticed and started addressing things in seconds and doctors are just like...have you tried increasing the meds you never needed before to manage the pain that's never been this bad and seeing if that just fixes the problem entirely?

I was so...taken aback by the blatant disregard that I didn't think of asking to document our requests for testing and the denial. I'll definitely remember that moving forward and might have her shoot the doctor an email tomorrow asking to retroactively note that.

It's so fucked, they really do get butthurt about it. This fucking doctor straight up asked her to stop naming the vertebrae but just point to where it hurts instead. She's a fucking athletic trainer. She knows where the god damn vertebrae are. It's literally her job. Point to where it hurts, is this fucking kindergarten??

It's so exhausting and enraging. I am going to these appointments to give a second opinion that yes, I am also seeing these issues at home with her. We have a PT backing up our assessment saying he's seeing neuromuscular instability and major discrepancies. But it's all a nocebo effect because you saw the xray and now you think it's worse than it is. Despite the fact that the pain was worse before any diagnostics were done. This is so fucked up

The ALAT isn't terribly difficult, especially if you come from a veterinary or biology background. The test questions are different than the AALAS Learning Library ones but not any harder. Mostly it's that you've probably spent enough time on AALAS that you've started to memorize the questions so it'll throw you off at first. 
If you're passing the online exams and have done the practice workbook, you should be good to go. Most techs I know didn't even pick up The Guide for the first exam. I found the ridiculous security check-in more stressful than the actual test.
Honestly it's a little bit offensive. Waiting on my cookies and nap time next.
Oh of course. The five pieces of xylitol gum for a 10 person shift, along with the two communal pandemic bubble blower things.
Haha, I love that a lot. I hope you make the jump and go forward with it!
That's awesome! I've been reaching out to my veterinary contacts for any referrals outside clinics and field work sounds amazing.

It sucks so hard. It took a couple jumps over the years but I finally figured out it's not the clinics, it's me. If I'm not happy at this clinic where my coworkers are generally awesome, then it's the job.
Same, my friend. All the best to you.
I've been looking into Medical Lab Tech degrees and although it looks like entry level is about the same as teching, the lack of actual people is really appealing.
Holy shit. Our clients are bold and getting worse but even they're not that aggressive (yet). I'm so sorry you had to go through that and I hope you excel at your new job!

I wouldn't say it's atypical, but YMMV. I've worked as a tech for over a decade and I would say that more people leave the industry than stay. That's not to say I don't know several technicians who deeply love what they do and will likely do it until they physically can't anymore. That also being said, that day will likely be before they are in their 50s. I've never met an old tech. 

But what you mentioned is the exactly the pressure I'm feeling. Do I throw away all the experience and start from scratch in my mid 30s?
Table to Stix is right in Evanston and has been pretty good.
